ELECTIONS GUIDE 2024

By: Nicky Troll | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
National Elections are less than 90 days away, but are you ready to make your mark South Africa – we give you the lowdown on some of the promises being peddled.

Summary:
2024 – the year of elections. Almost half the world’s population will go to the ballot boxes across about 80 countries.

In South Africa, the country is at cross road – politically and economically. It’s about survival – for the political parties and the people.

In this piece, we give viewers a quick overview what’s to come and what’s on offer.


Further information:
SCENE SETTER STATS // STATUS QUO
 XX REGISTERED VOTERS
 XX VOTING STATIONS
 MOONSHOT PACT?
 372 NATIONAL PARTIES

ELEMENTS
 What to expect in the voting booth – SHOW & TELL WITH THE IEC
 Manifesto BELIEVABLITY – promises vs commitments – GOVAN & MASA break it down and compare notes.
 What does it mean
o VOX POPS – SOWETO (MASA) // GOVAN?
o EXPERT VOICE – NOT THE USUAL SUSPECTS – TO BRING HOME
 Are you registered to vote?
 Are you voting for the person, the party or the promise?

THEMES
 MANIFESTOS – BEEN HERE, GOT THE T-SHIRT – BUT HAVE THEY DONE THAT?
Delivery on Promises?
 SURVIVAL


THE PARTIES & THE PROMISE – COMPARING NOTES SCENE
Many election manifesto pledges amount to nothing more than blatant lies and populist rhetoric, specifically targeting frustrated and vulnerable communities.
LET’s BREAK IT DOWN
THE BIG THREE & SLOGANS FOR 2024
 ANC – LET’s DO MORE TOGETHER
 DA – READY TO RESCUE SA
 EFF – LAND & JOBS NOW

THE NEWBIES
 ACTION SA
 MK Party
 RISE
 BOSA
 BIG

THE INDEPENDENTS
** I DUNNO WHO THEY ARE OR WHERE TO FIND ACTUAL DETAIL ON THEM – I’ve looked online – but nothing decent.

THE OTHERS
** WHAT DO WE SAY ABOUT THE IFP / VF / UDM / COPE / PAC? THEY’RE NOT SMALL BUT NOT THE BIG THREE EITHER?

MANIFESTOS – TOP PICKS
- JOBS
- LOADSHEDDING
- CRIME
- LAND
- IMMIGRATION
- INFRASTRUCTURE
- SOCIAL GRANTS
- CABINET REDUCTION / CORRUPTION / LEADERSHIP

There are so many other issues that divide and unite the country but these ones seem to be top of mind for everyone.


INTERVIEWS
- MASA – IEC SHOW & TELL – SET THE STAGE FOR 29 MAY
- MASA – VOX POPS SOWETO
- GOVAN – EXPERT VOICE TBC – either INSTITUTE FOR ECONOMIC JUSTICE – or MY VOTE COUNTS – MAKE SENSE OF MANIFESTO PROMISES AND REALISTIC LIKELIHOOD OF THESE PLEDGES.
- GOVAN – VOX POPS SANDTON
- MASA & GOVAN – VOX POPS IN BRAAM (IN THE DAY ) AROUND WITS?

** AIMING FOR 10 usuable VOX POPS
** EXPERT VOICE in A NEIGHBOURHOOD like Windsor maybe

VOX POP QUESTIONS
1. Have you registered to vote this year?
2. Are you voting for the person on the poster, the party or the promise?
3. Manisfesto Points (TBC) – we’ll focus on three

FINAL SCRIPT: ELECTIONS 2024

M VO: In just 80 days, South Africans head to the polls in the 7th national democratic election – possibly, the most pivotal since 1994.

DOUBLE PRESENTER OPENING LINK
GOVAN: It's a big year for the country. Some new political parties may make it to parliament.
MASA: While others may lose some existing power. The pressure is on.
GOVAN: Not just for the parties, but for the voters who want the promises made to them to be kept.
MASA: So we're on a mission to gain a better understanding of what to expect.
GOVAN: And who to believe.


M VO: In 2024, nearly half the world’s population will vote in elections in 80 countries. In South Africa, a record number of [27 757 747] voters have registered.

GOVAN LINK: For the parties in Parliament. This election is about survival for those contesting for the first time. It's about breaking the mould. But for South Africans, it's about change

G VO: KEAMOGETSWE SEIPATO is from MY VOTE COUNTS – an organization building an informed citizenry that takes part in democracy.

KEA: We see 2024 as a year of uncertainty, those possibilities of shifting power. So that's what makes it amazing.
GOVAN: OH! Every, every election cycle, they say that..
KEA: No, they lied
GOVAN: This is the year.
KEA: This is Year
GOVAN: Oh, come on.
KEA: // I can definitely tell you that there's opportunities to shift power this time if we do it correctly
GOVAN: 30 years of democracy – does it mean anything with unemployment, the way it is right now and loadshedding terrorizing communities.
KEA: The social and political implications of a country don't necessarily mean that we should give up on democracy. // there's a lot of work to be done to make democracy work for people.

G VO: BUT the burning question is what are people voting for?

VOX POPS: PERSON / PARTY / PROMISES….
Fast pace sequence – mosaic collage of people…. Bring one to the focal point on screen & audio up.
MADISHE: //Previously I was voting for the party, but and I think now it's more to do with what the individual presents.
MFUNDO: //We live in a world of political cults and personality cults. So it's always a party
NITHIN: //It's a mixture of all three but more the promise.

MASA: But what can we expect when we line up on the 29th of May to make our mark? The Independent Electoral Commission is running the show and they're going to give us a sneak peek of what's to come.

M VO: MAWETHU MOSERY is from the IEC. [INTRO SEQUENCE OF MAWETHU]

MAWETHU: // For the first time in 2024, we will have three ballot papers. We will also have a independents, a contesting for these ten legislatures for the first time, // it's a new era beginning going forward.

M VO: The IEC is gearing up 23 000 voting stations around the country, aiming to deliver a quick and efficient voting experience.

MASA: What should voters expect – what are they going to get?
MAWETHU: We give you the ballot papers.
MASA: PAPERS!?!
MAWETHU: PAPERS! there's is paper. They are three! LAUGHS// Two are for the National Assembly. That would be the pink and the orange are for the national legislature. And then the blue is for the provincial legislature.

M VO: In other words the Pink and Orange ballots decide who'll sit in Parliament in Cape Town, and the blue one is for those who'll govern the provinces.

KEA: People need to understand that these are national and provincial elections and in essence what we're trying to do is to decide who makes decisions in relation to the money of the country. // at national level // that makes sense for where money is dispersed // at a local government level, who then do we choose to implement the things that were decided nationally?

G VO: But this time round – the country is spoilt for choice.

Q M - HOW MANY PARTIES [TIMELINE VP- NUMBERS]
ODWA: I think maybe about ten or something
CLAUDINE: all the small parties, but this is just popping up like nobody's business. JOSEPH: Is well over 50 or something like that? I guess.
G - It's more. Keep going.
JOSEPH: Yeah. 60,
G – more
JOSEPH: 70, 80, 120 00:07:25:17 - 00:07:34:08

G VO: NO, THINK AGAIN…. There are over 350 national political parties that could contest this election.

ZHIMVUYO Yoh, that's a lot.
NANDU: I would never imagined that many
MFUNDO: Too much choice, is too many selections in might lead to voter apathy this year.

MASA: We have big three political parties. We have the usual. We also have the newbies and of course, the wild card. The introduction of independents. But in order to get onto the election ballot, it has to give notice to contests, pay at least a quarter of a million rand deposits and provide the list of signatures.

M VO: On election day, The Orange and Blue ballots will also vary from province to province and will include independent candidates for the first time in the country’s history.

The final list of qualifying political parties will be locked in by the end of March. But trends show, the number of voting options has yet to impact the outcome.

MAWETHU: Since 94 to now. We've not had more than 14 political parties sitting in the legislature, although contesting has been growing every election.

M VO: More than ever, the country’s ruling party is feeling the pressure with a majority win not guaranteed.

G VO: Unemployment at its highest, the economy is barely dodging a recession and the growing distrust in government’s capabilities is undeniable.

VP GENERAL

KEA: It's a crisis of neoliberalism and less of a crisis. Just special to South Africa.
GOVAN: Yeah, but what does what does that mean for people who are living through it? Most South African don't care that the same thing is happening in other countries. They just want stable electricity supply, stable water supply and a chance to improve their lives.
KEA: No, for sure you're right. People need to eat now. But understanding that it's not a special case in South Africa helps us think about the kind of solutions that we're wanting to put forth.

G VO: And solutions are a dime a dozen - when it comes to election time, parties launch extensive manifestos at elaborate events..

GOVAN: A manifesto is a contract of trust. The party sets out its promises and how they will fix our problems. But that manifesto isn't binding. It's really just a list. And the people know that. 00:00:50:12 - 00:01:04:07

G LOOKS AT THE TV SCREEN… clicks play…

VOX POPS MANIFESTO BELIEVABILITY
XOLANI: I guess it's just they are just telling us the dream.
REUBEN: // it's like it's not going to suddenly start raining houses and geysers and refrigerators of, you know, hard work is going to get this country back on its feet. MUSEFUWA: politicians are politicians. They make promises, but hopefully things will change.
KELLY: // We're here now because of the same promises that are being recycled.
DOROTHY: Every time when you go to vote. They promise? Promise, promise. Then after, they're gone

MANIFESTO PLAY OFFS
G VO: Election manifestos specifically target frustrated and vulnerable communities – honing in on daily struggles – selling a dream that many feel is long overdue.

MASA: So given lots of promises being made here, let's just talk through some of them.
GOVAN: Loadshedding, that's the biggest one. It's something that all the parties say they can solve some quicker than others.
MASA: Another big problem, unemployment, jobs. I mean, the ANC says they can provide up to three and a half million job opportunities. The data is two and a half million and the EFC is up to 9 million.
GOVAN: You know, it's a big election issue, corruption. South Africans are desperate for ethical leadership, but who can provide it?
MASA: Another thing that affects us all crime. Now, when it comes to crime, some are saying decentralize the police. And some are saying just tougher policing.
GOVAN: You know, there's so many other issues health, education, climate change. All of these parties say they've got solutions for these problems.
MASA: But are they plausible?

G VO - Word on the street is that South Africans are sceptical.

VP JOBS - TITLE: MILLIONS OF JOBS
LESEGO:, they are quite ambitious and obviously urged to get votes. // We can't just say 3 million or 9 million as in the EFF. How are you going to get 9 million jobs?
CORINA: LAUGHING I think all of that is impossible.
NITHIN: I'll take anything right now. It's like there's a lot of South Africans sitting and waiting. I’ll take anything for everyone.

LOADSHEDDING
MASA: Loadshedding - The EFF says they'll end it in six months.
BYRON: i think it’s impossible
GOVAN: Truth or lie.
KELLY&THOBILE: Lie, that's a lie.
XOLANI: LAUGHING – HOW?
MFUNDO: The faults load shedding have infested Eskom into its core. So it cannot be done by just throwing the money at it or just throwing policy at it. It's a much more complex.

M VO: But despite the distrust, there is still hope for change.

WAYNE: I think the cross is potentially very green if we keep watering it right way in the next couple of years, ahead of us.
THOBILE: it might take time, but you have to progressively try over and over again until something does change.

MAWETHU: When you go out there, you may be a single vote, but you doing it also on our behalf as a nation, as a country. 00:00:39:19 - 00:01:08:06

BOTH READ WHOLE BIT
M VO: Whether 2024 delivers change remains to be seen.

G VO: Perhaps most surprising right now, is how an obviously sceptical electorate is prepared to give politicians another chance to prove them wrong

END

PROMOS
PROMO 1
VO: A seminal national election less than 90 days away… South Africa, at a cross road – politically and economically.

VOX KELLY: We're here now because of the same promises that are being recycled.

VO: We hit the streets - questioning the promises being peddled and explore people’s expectations.


PROMO 2
VO: Promises, protests and power… South Africans are gearing up to make their mark in one of the country’s most important elections since 1994.

KEA: // I can definitely tell you that there's opportunities to shift power this time if we do it correctly

VO: We hit the streets to hear from the people. [COULD CUT END IF TOO LONG]


PROMO 3
VO: Politics, promises and the illusion of power… what will motivate South Africans to vote in the upcoming elections?

MAWETHU: When you go out there, you may be a single vote, but you doing it also on our behalf as a nation, as a country. 00:00:39:19 - 00:01:08:06

VO: We give you a quick overview of what’s to come and what’s on offer.

metadata.Summary: 2024 – the year of elections. Almost half the world’s population will go to the ballot boxes across about 80 countries. In South Africa, the country is at cross road – politically and economically. It’s about survival – for the political parties and the people. In this piece, we give viewers a quick overview what’s to come and what’s on offer.
